  • Linux Syscall Gate

Linux Syscall Gate

This chapter records the design direction for binary compatibility: Zephyr does not define a stable ABI of its own and never will. Separately-compiled applications instead target the stable ABI of another kernel - Linux - through a translation gate, the approach proven by FreeBSD’s Linux compatibility layer, NetBSD’s compat_linux, and illumos LX zones.

  • Model

  • Non-goals

  • Groundwork already in place

  • Gate architecture

  • Syscall tiers

  • clone3 mapping

  • Open questions

Model

Native APIs (sys_clone(), k_waitpid(), the k_sig_* family) remain honest internal interfaces: they may change shape in any release, because in-tree consumers rebuild with the kernel. The stability burden lands entirely on the gate, whose contract - syscall numbers, argument struct layouts, flag values, errno and signal numbering - is defined by Linux’s UAPI and therefore never has to be designed, versioned, or argued about here.

An important consequence for extensibility: native struct-taking syscalls do not need clone3-style size versioning. In-tree images rebuild; shipped images speak the gate, where Linux’s own extensible-struct contract (copy min(size, known), zero-fill the tail, reject a nonzero unknown tail with E2BIG) applies verbatim.

Non-goals

  • A Zephyr-native stable ABI. There is none and there will not be one.

  • Pseudo-file ABIs (/proc, /sys). File-based kernel interfaces are a separate concern with a separate stability story, deliberately out of scope here.

  • Namespaces, cgroups, ptrace, and checkpoint/restore (set_tid): no consumers, no plans.

Groundwork already in place

Much of the series was built with this destination in mind, and several pieces are already gate-shaped:

  • Thread-group processes. getpid()/gettid()/kill() semantics match Linux structurally: a process is its thread-group leader, any live member’s handle names the group, and kill() is process-directed while tgkill()-style delivery is thread-directed.

  • Handle-first identity. A k_pid_t is a handle with pidfd semantics - stable from creation to reap, immune to numeric reuse races. Linux spent a decade retrofitting exactly this (CLONE_PIDFD, pidfd_open(), waitid(P_PIDFD)) onto a numeric-pid world; the gate maps pidfds onto what is already the native identity model.

  • clone-shaped creation. sys_clone() took clone3’s lessons up front: struct-based arguments and 64-bit flags, with fork, spawn, and exec expressed as tiers (SYS_CLONE_VM_COPY, SYS_CLONE_PAUSED, thread restart) the way Linux expresses them over clone().

  • Numbering and errno. Signal numbering is Linux-aligned (SIGRTMIN), and builds already use __LINUX_ERRNO_EXTENSIONS__, so the errno translation is near-identity.

Gate architecture

Three pieces, all additive - nothing native changes shape for the gate:

Entry. A per-architecture Linux syscall number table and a dispatch path off the same trap instruction the native syscalls use. How a caller is recognized as a gate caller is an open question below.

Marshalling. The gate owns Linux UAPI struct definitions (its own headers, never leaked into native code), copies them in with Linux’s extensible-struct rules where Linux has them, and translates to native calls. Where a Linux struct and a native struct are close (clone_args vs sys_clone_args), the translation is a field-by-field copy; where Linux semantics have no native backing yet (exit_signal selection), the gate restricts rather than emulates: unsupported values fail loudly with EINVAL until a consumer justifies the plumbing.

Identity translation. The gate speaks Linux’s numeric pid/tid domain at the edge and resolves to handles internally via the existing sys-layer numbering (sys_process_id()/sys_process_find()). pidfds wrap handles in file descriptors using the K_OBJ_FILE infrastructure - which makes per-process descriptor tables a hard dependency of the pidfd tier.

Syscall tiers

Ordered by dependency, not ambition; each tier is independently useful and independently testable.

Tier

Syscalls

Native backing

0 - identity

getpid, getppid, gettid, kill, exit, exit_group, wait4, waitid

Direct: sys-layer numbering, k_kill(), k_exit(), k_waitpid(). gettid needs the numeric-tid extension of the numbering layer (today numbers cover processes only).

1 - creation

clone3 (thread and fork forms), execve

sys_clone() tiers; the exec machinery. The clone3 mapping is below; execve at the gate resolves through the same two-tier image resolution the POSIX layer uses.

2 - signals

rt_sigaction, rt_sigprocmask, rt_sigtimedwait, sigaltstack, tgkill

The k_sig_* family, which already follows Linux semantics for masks, process-directed delivery, and queueing.

3 - pidfd

CLONE_PIDFD, pidfd_open, pidfd_send_signal, waitid(P_PIDFD)

k_pid_t wrapped as a K_OBJ_FILE descriptor over the per-process descriptor tables.

later

futex, nanosleep/clock_*, mmap subset

k_futex (already user-address-capable), the clock/timer layer, PROCESS_VM machinery.

clone3 mapping

  • CLONE_VM|CLONE_THREAD|... (thread creation) maps to clone’s thread tier; the child starts at the given stack, as Linux threads do.

  • The fork form (no CLONE_VM) maps to SYS_CLONE_VM_COPY and the kernel-assisted resume.

  • exit_signal other than SIGCHLD is EINVAL until something needs it; set_tid and cgroup are EINVAL permanently (see non-goals).

  • CLONE_PIDFD is tier 3.

Open questions

  • Caller recognition. One trap instruction serves both ABIs. The leading candidate is a per-process personality: an image loaded through the exec loader is marked as a gate consumer at load time, and the syscall entry dispatches on the calling process’s mark rather than on anything in the trap itself. A dedicated second trap vector is the fallback where an architecture makes that cheap.

  • vDSO surface. Linux binaries expect gettimeofday-class calls to be cheap. Whether the gate needs a vDSO-like page or simply eats the trap cost is deferred until a real consumer exists.

  • Numeric tid ABI. The numbering layer numbers processes; gettid and tgkill need per-thread numbers. This is the identity-model extension flagged in the process design chapter as a separate milestone.

  • TLS setup for gate binaries. Linux’s clone3 accepts a tls pointer; native creation carves TLS with the stack. Gate thread creation must honor the caller-provided pointer, which the restart/fork machinery already proves is representable.

Dependencies and sequencing

  1. Numeric-tid extension of the sys-layer numbering (unblocks tier 0’s gettid and tier 2’s tgkill). Done.

  2. Per-process descriptor tables in zvfs (unblocks tier 3, and was independently the last declared POSIX deviation). Done.

  3. Clone unification (the thread tier on sys_clone()), so tier 1 maps onto one primitive instead of two. Done, with k_clone() beneath it as the allocation-free kernel primitive.

  4. The gate itself, tier by tier, each tier landing with a Linux-binary-shaped test image exec’d through the loader.
